quiz.q: What lactate value triggers the 30 mL/kg fluid bolus in a normotensive septic patient?
choices: 1.0 or more
1.5 or more
4 or more
Any measurable lactate
quiz.why: A lactate of 4 or more marks severe illness and triggers the bolus even without hypotension. Values at or below 2 are normal, and treating every measurable lactate would give large fluid volumes to patients who do not need them.

quiz.q: A septic patient's MAP is 58 after 30 mL/kg of crystalloid. What comes next?
choices: Another 30 mL/kg bolus before anything else
Vasopressor support, typically norepinephrine
Repeat the lactate and wait for the result
Withhold further treatment until blood cultures grow
quiz.why: A MAP under 65 that persists after adequate fluid defines septic shock and calls for vasopressors. Repeating the full bolus risks fluid overload, and no one waits days for culture growth before supporting a pressure.

quiz.q: A trauma patient has been fully exposed for the primary survey. What is the immediate next priority?
choices: Warm blankets and active warming measures
Obtain a detailed medication history
Send the patient to CT
Place a urinary catheter
quiz.why: Hypothermia impairs clotting and is part of the lethal triad, so warming follows exposure immediately. History, imaging and catheters all come after the primary survey priorities are addressed.

quiz.q: Which IV access is appropriate for a level-one trauma activation?
choices: One 22 gauge in the hand
One 20 gauge in the forearm
A single 18 gauge and a saline lock
Two 14-16 gauge lines in the antecubital fossae
quiz.why: Large-bore access in two sites allows rapid volume and blood product delivery, since flow depends heavily on catheter diameter. Smaller or single lines cannot deliver a massive transfusion at the needed rate.

quiz.q: A 22-year-old motorcyclist has a heart rate of 124 and a blood pressure of 118/76 after a high-speed crash. How do you interpret the vitals?
choices: Both are normal, so significant injury is unlikely
The tachycardia is expected anxiety and can be disregarded
He is compensating and may be bleeding despite a normal pressure
A normal blood pressure excludes internal bleeding
quiz.why: Young patients maintain blood pressure through vasoconstriction and tachycardia until a large volume is lost, then drop abruptly. Attributing the tachycardia to anxiety or trusting the pressure is how hemorrhage gets missed.

quiz.q: A patient who overdosed on opioids is breathing 5 times per minute. What is the goal of naloxone therapy?
choices: Complete reversal of all sedation
Reversal of the pupils to normal size
Adequate ventilation, achieved with titrated doses
A single large dose so no repeat is needed
quiz.why: The therapeutic endpoint is breathing, not wakefulness. Full reversal precipitates withdrawal, agitation and vomiting, and pupil size is not the target. Naloxone is shorter-acting than most opioids, so repeat dosing is expected regardless.

quiz.q: A tricyclic antidepressant overdose patient has a QRS of 130 ms. Why does this matter?
choices: It confirms the ingestion was small
It indicates a normal conduction system
It is unrelated to the overdose
A widening QRS predicts seizures and arrhythmia
quiz.why: QRS widening reflects sodium channel blockade. Over 100 ms predicts seizures and over 160 ms predicts arrhythmia, so 130 ms is a marker of serious toxicity, not reassurance or an incidental finding.

quiz.q: A somnolent patient arrives 3 hours after a mixed ingestion. Someone suggests activated charcoal. What is the problem?
choices: He is outside the useful window and cannot protect his airway
Charcoal is ineffective against all ingestions
Charcoal requires a nasogastric tube in every case
Charcoal must be paired with naloxone
quiz.why: Charcoal is generally useful within about an hour and only in an awake patient who can protect the airway, because aspirated charcoal is devastating. It does bind many substances, and neither an NG tube nor naloxone is a universal requirement.

quiz.q: A patient ingested acetaminophen at 10:00 and arrives at 11:30. A level drawn now returns as low. What does that tell you?
choices: The ingestion was not significant and he can go home
The antidote can safely be withheld
Nothing usable; the level must be repeated at 14:00 for the nomogram
He should receive activated charcoal instead of a repeat level
quiz.why: The treatment nomogram is only valid from 4 hours post-ingestion, once absorption is complete, so an early level cannot exclude toxicity. Discharging or withholding the antidote on that basis risks fatal liver failure.

quiz.q: A 19-year-old collapsed while sprinting, with no warning symptoms. Which action is most important?
choices: Reassure him that exertional fainting is common in athletes
Obtain a 12-lead ECG and report the exertional, prodrome-free history
Give oral fluids and discharge once he feels better
Obtain orthostatic vitals only
quiz.why: Exertional syncope without a prodrome suggests a structural or electrical cardiac cause, and the ECG is the single test that changes management. Reassurance, fluids and orthostatics alone miss hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and inherited conduction disease.

quiz.q: How long should a patient lie supine before the first orthostatic measurement?
choices: No rest period is required
30 seconds
2 minutes
5 minutes
quiz.why: Five minutes supine establishes a true baseline, and readings are then taken at 1 and 3 minutes standing. Shorter or absent rest periods produce numbers that cannot be interpreted as orthostatic changes.

quiz.q: A 44-year-old says her headache went from nothing to maximum severity in about five seconds. What is the immediate concern and workup?
choices: Subarachnoid hemorrhage; CT head, then lumbar puncture if the CT is negative
Tension headache; oral analgesia and discharge
Sinusitis; antibiotics and follow-up
Migraine; dark room and the standard cocktail without imaging
quiz.why: A thunderclap onset is subarachnoid hemorrhage until CT and, if negative, lumbar puncture prove otherwise. Tension and sinus headaches build gradually, and treating this as a migraine without imaging misses a ruptured aneurysm.

quiz.q: What rectal temperature defines fever in an infant?
quiz.why: 38.0°C, or 100.4°F, is the threshold that drives the entire infant fever algorithm. Lower values are not fever, and setting the bar higher would miss infants who need a full evaluation.

quiz.q: A 20-day-old with a rectal temperature of 38.4°C is smiling, feeding well, and has normal vital signs. What is expected?
choices: Discharge with 24-hour follow-up
Blood and urine studies only, then discharge if normal
Full evaluation including lumbar puncture, with admission and antibiotics
Antipyretics and reassessment in 2 hours
quiz.why: Under 28 days, a well appearance does not lower the risk of bacteremia or meningitis, so the full workup including LP is standard. Partial workups and observation strategies miss infections in infants who look deceptively well.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old with two weeks of back pain now reports numbness when he wipes and says he has not urinated since yesterday. What do you do?
choices: Tell the provider immediately and prepare for a post-void residual bladder scan
Provide oral analgesia and arrange outpatient follow-up
Obtain plain lumbar films and wait
Encourage fluids and reassess in two hours
quiz.why: Saddle anesthesia with urinary retention is cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency that needs urgent MRI and decompression. Analgesia, plain films and watchful waiting all lose the window in which function can be preserved.

quiz.q: In DKA, which order of treatment is correct?
choices: Insulin drip first, then fluids
Insulin and bicarbonate together
Potassium replacement before any fluid
Fluids first, then the insulin drip
quiz.why: The patient is profoundly volume depleted, fluid alone lowers glucose substantially, and insulin into an empty tank worsens perfusion and drops potassium dangerously. Bicarbonate is not routine and potassium is guided by serial levels.

quiz.q: A DKA patient's initial potassium is 5.4. Two hours into the insulin drip the cardiac monitor shows new changes. What is the likely explanation?
choices: The glucose has risen
The patient is developing hypercalcemia
Insulin has driven potassium into cells and the level has fallen
The bicarbonate has normalized
quiz.why: Total body potassium is depleted in DKA even when the serum level looks high, and insulin shifts it intracellularly, causing a rapid drop with cardiac consequences. That is exactly why a monitor and a BMP every 2-4 hours are standard.

quiz.q: A patient with hives and wheezing after eating shellfish has a blood pressure of 84/48. Which is given first?
choices: Intravenous famotidine
Intramuscular epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg in the outer thigh
Intravenous methylprednisolone
A 1 L normal saline bolus
quiz.why: Epinephrine is the only agent that reverses airway swelling and vasodilation, and delay is the leading cause of death in anaphylaxis. Antihistamines, steroids and fluids are adjuncts given after epinephrine, not instead of it.

scenarios.title: Walk-in at the desk: 'My chest hurts'
scenarios.intro: It is 15:40 on a busy Tuesday. Every room is full and there are nine people in the waiting room. A `58-year-old` man walks up to the triage window, pale and sweating through his shirt, and says his chest has felt heavy for about `45 minutes`. He drove himself. You are the tech at the front.

steps.prompt: He is standing at the window, one hand on his sternum. The triage nurse is mid-assessment with another patient. What do you do?

choices.text: Bring the ECG machine to him and get a 12-lead immediately
choices.feedback: Correct. The 10-minute clock started when he arrived. The machine moves to the patient, not the other way around, and you do not wait for registration or a room.

choices.text: Have him sign in and take a seat while you find the nurse
choices.feedback: This is the delay that kills. Every minute of a blocked coronary artery is muscle lost, and a waiting-room chair is where undiagnosed STEMIs sit.

choices.text: Walk him to a hallway bed and take a full set of vitals first
choices.feedback: Getting him off his feet is good, but vitals are not the time-critical test. The ECG comes first and the vitals happen while it prints.

choices.text: Tell the charge nurse there is a chest pain at the window, then get the ECG machine
choices.feedback: Announcing it is genuinely useful, and doing it on your way to the machine loses nothing. Just do not let the announcement replace the tracing.

steps.prompt: You have him on a stretcher in the hallway, shirt off, leads on. The tracing prints at 15:46. You can see obvious ST elevation across several leads.

choices.text: Carry the tracing directly to a provider and say 'chest pain ECG, ST elevation'
choices.feedback: Exactly right. An ECG on the machine is worthless. Putting it in a provider's hand with those words starts the cath lab activation.

choices.text: Leave it on the machine and go tell the nurse there is an abnormal ECG
choices.feedback: The tracing has to physically reach a provider. Second-hand descriptions delay activation by minutes that matter.

choices.text: Scan it into the chart so the provider sees it when they open the record
choices.feedback: Charting is not communication. In a possible STEMI you hand the paper over and say it out loud.

choices.text: Repeat the ECG first to make sure it was not artifact
choices.feedback: Understandable instinct, but a provider can distinguish artifact in seconds. Show them this one now and repeat afterward if they ask.

steps.prompt: The provider looks at the tracing and calls a STEMI alert. Time is 15:48. She asks you to get the room ready while the nurse gets aspirin into him. What do you set up?

choices.text: Cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry, automatic blood pressure, and two 18-20 gauge IVs with the troponin and other labs drawn on the stick
choices.feedback: That is the package. Two lines because the cath lab wants access, and labs on the stick so nobody sticks him twice.

choices.text: One IV, since the cath lab will place their own access anyway
choices.feedback: Two lines are the standard for a STEMI, and the cath lab expects usable peripheral access on arrival. One line leaves no margin if it fails.

choices.text: Monitor and a non-rebreather at 15 L, since his saturation is 96%
choices.feedback: Oxygen is only indicated under a saturation of 90%. At 96% it provides no benefit and high-flow oxygen may cause harm through vasoconstriction.

choices.text: Monitor and IVs, and get the chest X-ray started in the room
choices.feedback: Reasonable, and a portable film is part of the workup, but it never delays the cath lab. Access and monitoring come first.

steps.prompt: Everything is in. He suddenly says the pain just got much worse and he feels sick. Time is 15:54.

choices.text: Repeat the 12-lead immediately and tell the provider the pain changed and the pressure dropped
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts. Any change in symptoms earns a repeat ECG, and a falling pressure with rising heart rate in a STEMI is a report you make out loud right now.

choices.text: Reassure him and give him an emesis bag
choices.feedback: The bag is kind, but nausea with worsening pain and a dropping pressure is a deterioration, not a comfort problem.

choices.text: Recheck the blood pressure manually before saying anything
choices.feedback: Verifying an abnormal automated pressure is good practice, but do it while you are calling the provider, not instead of it.

choices.text: Note the new vitals in the chart and continue preparing for transport
choices.feedback: Charting a deterioration without announcing it means nobody acts on it. Say it, then chart it.

steps.prompt: The cath lab calls to say they are ready. The provider asks you to help with transport. Time is 16:04, `24 minutes` after he walked up to the desk.

choices.text: Transport on the monitor with oxygen and suction on the bed, a provider or nurse at the head, and the defibrillator with the patient
choices.feedback: Right. A patient having an acute infarct can arrest in the elevator. He travels monitored, escorted, and with the equipment to treat it.

choices.text: Transport quickly on the stretcher without the monitor to save time
choices.feedback: Disconnecting the monitor for a four-minute trip is when ventricular fibrillation happens unwitnessed. The monitor goes with him.

choices.text: Wait for a transport tech so you can stay at the desk
choices.feedback: A STEMI in progress is not a routine transport. This patient goes now, with clinical staff.

choices.text: Confirm the tracing, the chart and the labs went with him, then move with the team
choices.feedback: A useful habit, since the cath lab wants the ECG in hand, but it is a step alongside monitored transport rather than a substitute for it.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern is **ECG in 10 minutes, into a hand, and repeat with any change.** Everything else in a STEMI is downstream of those three things, and all three are the tech's job. He was never registered before the tracing was taken, and that is correct: the clock starts at arrival, not at check-in. Notice what did not happen. He did not get oxygen at a saturation of `96%`, because routine oxygen in a non-hypoxic patient is not helpful. He did get two `18-20 gauge` IVs with the labs drawn at the same time, because the cath lab wants access and nobody should be stuck twice. And when his pain changed at 15:54, the response was a repeat ECG plus a spoken report, not a note in the chart. Door to cath lab in `24 minutes` is a team result, but the first `6` of those minutes belonged to one person with an ECG machine.

scenarios.title: EMS handoff: 84-year-old from a nursing home, 'not acting right'
scenarios.intro: EMS rolls in with an `84-year-old` woman from a skilled nursing facility. The transfer paper says "altered mental status, decreased oral intake for two days." The medic reports she normally talks and feeds herself, and today she is confused and will not wake fully. She has a chronic indwelling urinary catheter. You are assigned to the room with one nurse.

steps.prompt: She is moved onto the bed. She opens her eyes to voice but does not answer questions. Her skin is warm and mottled at the knees.

choices.text: Report the full vitals out loud and say the words 'possible sepsis' to the nurse and provider
choices.feedback: Correct. Confusion, tachycardia, a low temperature and a soft pressure is the elderly septic picture. Naming it out loud is what starts the bundle.

choices.text: Chart the vitals and wait for the provider to come assess
choices.feedback: These numbers are a bundle trigger. Quietly charting them wastes the hour that matters most.

choices.text: Recheck the temperature, since 35.5°C is probably a bad reading
choices.feedback: Confirming an odd value is fine, but do not dismiss it. Hypothermia in sepsis is as ominous as fever, and older adults often do not mount one.

choices.text: Get her on the monitor and start a full set of vitals including a repeat blood pressure
choices.feedback: Good and necessary, but it is not enough by itself. The pattern needs to be said out loud to the team.

steps.prompt: The provider agrees and calls a sepsis alert. The order set is in: lactate, blood cultures times two, broad-spectrum antibiotics, `30 mL/kg` crystalloid, urinalysis and urine culture, CBC, metabolic panel, coagulation studies. She weighs `60 kg`. What do you do first?

choices.text: Establish two IVs and draw the blood cultures and the lactate with the stick, before anything goes into the lines
choices.feedback: Exactly. Your draw is the rate-limiting step for the entire bundle, because the antibiotic is waiting on those cultures.

choices.text: Start the antibiotic first, since time to antibiotics drives mortality
choices.feedback: Antibiotics do drive mortality, but giving them before cultures can leave the team without an organism and the patient on the wrong drug for days. Draw fast, then hang.

choices.text: Hang the fluid first and draw the cultures once it is running
choices.feedback: Fluids are important but not ahead of cultures, and drawing through a line that has been flushed risks a diluted or contaminated sample.

choices.text: Get the urine sample from the catheter bag first, since she already has a catheter
choices.feedback: The urine is needed, but not from the bag. That is stagnant, colonized urine. Sample from the port after cleaning it, and do it after the blood cultures.

steps.prompt: Two `18 gauge` lines are in. Cultures from two separate sites are drawn and labeled, and the rest of the blood is off to the lab. The nurse is ready with the antibiotic. How much fluid does she get, and how?

choices.text: About 1.8 L of crystalloid, run wide open
choices.feedback: Correct. 30 mL/kg times 60 kg is 1,800 mL, and it is given rapidly rather than on a slow maintenance rate.

choices.text: 1 L over four hours on a pump
choices.feedback: Both the volume and the rate are wrong. A slow liter does not restore perfusion in a vasodilated septic patient.

choices.text: About 1.8 L, but hold it until the lactate returns
choices.feedback: She is already hypotensive, which is its own indication. Waiting on the lactate wastes the hour.

choices.text: 500 mL, then reassess her pressure before giving more
choices.feedback: Cautious, and reassessment is right, but the guideline-directed initial volume is 30 mL/kg for hypotension. Small boluses under-resuscitate her.

steps.prompt: The lactate comes back at `4.6`. The fluid is running. The provider asks you to get the urine sample and keep an eye on her. What is your plan?

choices.text: Sample from the catheter's sampling port after disinfecting it, and take vitals at least every 15 minutes
choices.feedback: Right on both. A port sample reflects current urine, and frequent vitals are how a falling MAP gets caught early.

choices.text: Sample from the drainage bag and check vitals hourly
choices.feedback: Bag urine is stagnant and colonized, so the culture is unreliable, and hourly vitals are far too infrequent for a patient with a lactate of 4.6.

choices.text: Ask whether the chronic catheter should be changed before the sample is taken
choices.feedback: A genuinely good question, since a long-standing catheter is a likely source and is often exchanged. Raise it, then still get a usable sample and keep monitoring.

choices.text: Skip the urine, since the catheter itself is the obvious source
choices.feedback: The suspected source still needs a culture to guide the antibiotic, and assuming the source without testing is how the real one gets missed.

steps.prompt: Forty minutes later the fluid is nearly through. Her repeat blood pressure is 88/46, giving a MAP around `60`. She is still confused.

choices.text: Report the MAP under 65 to the provider immediately, since vasopressors are likely next
choices.feedback: Correct. A MAP under 65 that persists after adequate fluid defines septic shock, and norepinephrine is the usual next step. You are the one who noticed it.

choices.text: Wait for the fluid to finish and recheck in 30 minutes
choices.feedback: She has had nearly the full 30 mL/kg and is still hypoperfusing. Another 30 minutes of watching is 30 minutes of organ ischemia.

choices.text: Ask whether a repeat lactate should be drawn
choices.feedback: A reasonable question, since a repeat is due at 2-4 hours when the first was elevated. But the MAP is the urgent finding and it goes first.

choices.text: Raise the head of the bed to help her breathing and recheck the pressure
choices.feedback: Sitting a hypotensive patient up can drop the pressure further. Report the MAP rather than repositioning her.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern is **recognize, draw, hang, watch.** Recognition was the hard part and it was not a fever: confusion, a heart rate of `116`, a temperature of `35.5°C` and a soft pressure. Older adults arrive hypothermic and quiet, and the team that waits for a fever loses the hour. The sequencing inside the bundle is the part techs own. **Blood cultures times two from separate sites before antibiotics**, because once the drug is in, the organism may never grow. Then the lactate, then `30 mL/kg` which is `1.8 L` at `60 kg`, run wide open rather than pumped slowly. Urine came from the sampling port and not the bag, because bag urine is stagnant and its culture cannot be trusted. And the finding that changed the plan at the end was a **MAP under `65` after full fluids**, which is the definition of septic shock and the trigger for vasopressors. That number came from a set of vitals somebody took on time.

scenarios.title: Trauma activation: motorcycle versus car, 26-year-old
scenarios.intro: The radio call comes in `6 minutes` out: `26-year-old` male, motorcycle versus car at highway speed, helmeted, ejected from the bike, prolonged extrication. Awake on scene but confused. Two large-bore IVs attempted in the field with one successful. A tourniquet was placed on the right thigh at 18:12 for heavy bleeding from an open wound. A full trauma activation is called. You are assigned the **exposure and access** role.

steps.prompt: You have `6 minutes` before arrival. The team is gowning up. What do you do with the time?

choices.text: Set up your station: trauma shears, warm blankets and the fluid warmer, two large-bore IV kits, and the blood tubes including type and cross
choices.feedback: Exactly. Every second you spend hunting for equipment after arrival is a second the primary survey stalls. Set up to your assigned role.

choices.text: Wait by the door so you can help move the patient off the stretcher
choices.feedback: You will help with the transfer, but standing empty-handed wastes six minutes of preparation you will wish you had.

choices.text: Prepare the CT scanner and call radiology to hold a slot
choices.feedback: Someone will do this, but it is not your role and it is not the first minutes. Imaging comes after the primary survey.

choices.text: Draw up medications so they are ready when needed
choices.feedback: Medications are the nurse's scope, not yours, and preparing drugs outside your role creates a real safety problem.

steps.prompt: He arrives at 18:31. EMS gives the handoff. He is moved across on the count. He is confused, moving all four limbs, with an obvious deformed right thigh and the tourniquet in place. The team leader calls "exposure."

choices.text: Cut away all clothing front and back including shoes, then immediately cover him with warm blankets and start the warmer
choices.feedback: Correct, and the second half is the half people forget. You uncover him to find injuries, then cover him right back up, because cold patients stop clotting.

choices.text: Cut away the clothing and leave him uncovered so the team can keep examining him
choices.feedback: This is how trauma patients become hypothermic. Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy feed each other, and a cold patient bleeds more.

choices.text: Remove only the clothing over the injured leg to keep him warm
choices.feedback: Partial exposure hides injuries. A back wound, a second penetrating injury or a hidden fracture gets missed. Everything comes off, then everything gets covered.

choices.text: Cut the clothing away, save it for police, and cover him with warm blankets
choices.feedback: Right on all three. Full exposure, immediate warming, and clothing preserved because it may be evidence in a collision investigation.

steps.prompt: The team leader calls for access and labs. He has one field IV in the left forearm that is running. What do you do?

choices.text: Place a second large-bore line, 14-16 gauge, in an antecubital fossa and draw type and cross, CBC, metabolic panel, coagulation studies, lactate and a blood gas with it
choices.feedback: Correct. Two large-bore lines and a type and cross are the trauma standard, and drawing with the stick avoids a second needle.

choices.text: Place a 20 gauge in the hand as a backup line
choices.feedback: A small distal line will not deliver blood products at the rate a bleeding patient needs. Flow depends heavily on catheter diameter.

choices.text: Use the existing field line for the labs and skip the second IV
choices.feedback: One line is not enough for a patient who may need massive transfusion, and a single field IV can fail at exactly the wrong moment.

choices.text: Place the second large-bore line but wait for the provider to specify which labs
choices.feedback: The access is right, and asking is never wrong, but the trauma panel including type and cross is standard and predictable. Draw it and confirm.

steps.prompt: The FAST exam is being done. The team leader calls for a log roll. His blood pressure has drifted to 98/60 with a heart rate of 136. Someone says the tourniquet looks like it has loosened and there is fresh blood on the sheet.

choices.text: Announce the fresh bleeding and the vital signs out loud, and be ready to tighten or place a second tourniquet on the provider's direction
choices.feedback: Correct. A loosening tourniquet with a rising heart rate and falling pressure is an immediate, spoken finding, not something to handle silently.

choices.text: Remove the tourniquet, since it has been on for about 20 minutes
choices.feedback: Tourniquets are released deliberately by the team when the patient is resuscitated and ready, never because time has passed. Removing it here restarts the bleeding.

choices.text: Tighten it yourself immediately without saying anything
choices.feedback: The action may be right but the silence is not. In a trauma bay every finding and every intervention is called out so the team leader can build the picture.

choices.text: Continue with the log roll first, since the leader called for it
choices.feedback: Active bleeding outranks the log roll. Say what you are seeing; the leader will re-order the tasks.

steps.prompt: Bleeding is controlled, the log roll is done, and the FAST shows free fluid in the abdomen. The team activates the massive transfusion protocol and prepares to move to CT. The leader asks you to run for blood.

choices.text: Take the paperwork, bring the cooler, verify each unit against the patient, and know that the protocol runs red cells, plasma and platelets 1:1:1
choices.feedback: That is the runner role done properly. Balanced ratios exist because a bleeding patient loses whole blood, and every unit must be tracked and verified.

choices.text: Bring only red cells, since that is what replaces blood loss
choices.feedback: Red cells alone dilute clotting factors and platelets and worsen coagulopathy. The 1:1:1 ratio is the entire point of a massive transfusion protocol.

choices.text: Go for the blood but skip the verification to save time
choices.feedback: Transfusion verification is never skipped. A wrong unit in a bleeding patient is a fatal event, and it takes seconds to check.

choices.text: Ask whether tranexamic acid has been given before you leave
choices.feedback: A sharp question, since TXA reduces death from bleeding when given within 3 hours of injury. Ask it on your way, but the blood is the urgent errand.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern is **prepare, expose and warm, access and draw, call out everything.** The role was assigned before the doors opened, which is why the first six minutes were spent setting up rather than watching. Exposure is one task with two halves: everything off to find injuries, then warm blankets and a warmer on, because hypothermia with acidosis and coagulopathy is the lethal triad and a cold patient will not clot. Access means **two large-bore lines, `14-16 gauge`**, with **type and cross** drawn on the stick, because flow rate depends on catheter diameter and blood products cannot be pushed through a hand IV. Two traps showed up. His blood pressure read `114/72` on arrival with a heart rate of `128`, and a young patient holds that pressure right up until he does not. And the field tourniquet stayed on: tourniquets come off when the team decides, not when the clock says so. Finally, everything you see gets said out loud. A finding nobody hears is a finding nobody acts on.
